samples.guide: Use familiar concrete words, explicit subjects, one idea per clause and clear repetition. Use correct case, aspect and agreement. Cyrillic only, without Latin transliteration or added stress marks.
samples.brief: Two friends at a railway station discover their tickets are for different destinations.
samples.sourceChapter:
Анна и Иван на вокзале. У Анны маленькая сумка. У Ивана большой рюкзак. Друзья стоят рядом и ждут поезд.

Анна достаёт билет.

— У меня есть билет. Я еду в Москву, — говорит Анна.

Иван тоже достаёт билет.

— У меня есть билет. Я еду в Казань, — говорит Иван.

Анна смотрит на Ивана.

— В Казань? Но мы едем вместе!

— Да, вместе, в Москву, — говорит Иван.

Иван смотрит на свой билет ещё раз. На билете слово «Казань».

Анна показывает свой билет. На её билете слово «Москва».

— У нас разные билеты, — говорит Анна. — Я еду в Москву, а ты едешь в Казань.

— Да. Это разные города, — говорит Иван.

Рядом стоит поезд. Иван смотрит на поезд, потом на Анну.

— Анна, что мы теперь делаем?

content.title: У кассы
content.story:
— Давай пойдём в кассу, — говорит Анна. — Касса там.

Анна показывает на окно. Над окном слово «Касса».

Иван берёт рюкзак. Друзья идут к кассе. За окном сидит женщина.

— Здравствуйте, — говорит Иван. — Я хочу ехать в Москву. Но у меня билет в Казань.

Иван показывает билет. Женщина смотрит на билет.

— Да, это билет в Казань, — говорит она.

— У меня билет в Москву, — говорит Анна. — Мы хотим ехать вместе.

Анна тоже показывает билет.

Женщина смотрит на экран.

— В Москву есть другой поезд. Он идёт вечером.

— А этот поезд? — спрашивает Иван.

— На этот поезд билетов нет, — говорит женщина.

Иван смотрит на Анну.

— Я могу поехать вечером. А ты?

Анна кладёт свой билет на стол.

— Я тоже хочу поехать вечером. У вас есть два билета?

Женщина снова смотрит на экран. Анна и Иван ждут у кассы.

glossary.meaning: Introduces a suggestion: 'let’s.' Used when speaking to one person.
To go or set off on foot. Пойдём means 'let’s go' here.
To; followed by the accusative case to show a destination.
Ticket office or ticket counter. Касса is the subject form; кассу follows в for a destination; кассе follows к; кассы follows у.
To say or speak. Говорит means 'says,' with one person as the subject.
There; indicates where the ticket counter is.
To show a ticket or point something out. Показывает is the present-tense form for one person.
To point at something; here, to point at the window.
Window, here the ticket-counter window. Окно follows на when pointing at it; окном follows над and за for location.
Above; над окном means 'above the window.' Uses the instrumental case.
A word; here, the word on the sign.
To take or pick up. Берёт means 'takes' or 'picks up.'
Backpack; here, the bag Ivan picks up.
Friend. Друзья is the irregular plural: 'friends.'
To go on foot. Идут means 'they are walking'; идёт describes a train running or departing.
To or towards; к кассе means 'to the ticket counter.' Uses the dative case.
Behind; за окном means 'behind the window.' Uses the instrumental case for location.
To sit or be seated. Сидит describes one person sitting.
Woman; here, the woman working at the ticket counter.
Hello; a polite greeting used with a stranger.
I; the person speaking.
To want. Хочу means 'I want'; хотим means 'we want.' Followed here by an infinitive.
To travel by transport; here, to go by train. An imperfective infinitive after 'want.'
But; introduces the problem with Ivan’s ticket.
I have; literally, 'with me.' Меня is the genitive form of я. Есть can be omitted, as in у меня билет.
Ticket. Билет is singular; билета is used after два; билетов is genitive plural after нет.
To look at something or someone. На is followed here by the accusative case.
Yes; confirms what destination the ticket is for.
This or it, used to identify something: 'this is a ticket.' Russian does not need a present-tense word for 'is' here.
She; refers to the woman at the counter.
We; refers to the two friends together.
Together; travelling with one another.
Also or too; shows that Anna does the same thing or has the same wish.
Screen; here, the screen the woman checks.
There is or there are; also used in questions about having something available.
Another or a different one; describes an alternative train.
Train.
He or it; here, 'it' refers to поезд, a masculine noun.
In the evening; tells when the train runs and when the friends can travel.
And, but, or 'what about'; here, introduces a question about an alternative train or the other person.
This; points to the particular train already being discussed. Masculine singular to match поезд.
To ask a question. Спрашивает means 'asks.'
For this train; describes which train the tickets would be for.
There is none or there are none. Билетов нет means 'there are no tickets'; the noun uses the genitive case.
To be able to or can. Могу means 'I can' and is followed by an infinitive.
To go or set off by transport. A perfective infinitive, referring here to a planned train journey.
You, when speaking informally to one person.
What about you? A short question asking whether the other person can do the same.
To put or place something down. Кладёт means 'puts.'
One’s own; here, Anna’s own ticket. Agrees with the masculine noun билет.
Onto the table; на takes the accusative case for where something is being placed.
Table or desk; here, the surface where Anna puts her ticket.
Do you have? Here, вас is the polite form of 'you,' addressed to the woman.
Two. Before a masculine noun, два is followed by the genitive singular: два билета.
Again; the woman checks the screen another time.
And; joins the two friends’ names.
To wait. Ждут means 'they are waiting.'
At or by the ticket counter. У takes the genitive case.

materialIssues: «Давай пойдём в кассу» combines a suggestion construction with perfective future morphology; «Я могу поехать вечером» adds a modal plus perfective infinitive. These increase beginner grammatical load, although the notes explain them well.
«А этот поезд?» has an identifiable reference to the train in the preceding scene, but its destination remains unspecified. Explicitly identifying it would make the ticket problem easier to follow.

«идёт» is glossed as a train 'running or departing.' In «Он идёт вечером», running or travelling in the evening is supported; a specific departure meaning is less precise and would normally be expressed with «отправляется». This is a gloss precision issue, not a grammatical error.
strengths: Short clauses, repeated explicit names and concrete station actions closely follow the supplied guide.
The notes accurately explain contextual case forms, irregular plurals, possession, agreement and the distinction between walking and transport verbs.
Broad common-word support is useful here; overlapping lemma and phrase notes generally serve distinct explanatory purposes.
The continuation logically seeks alternative tickets and ends with a natural unresolved availability question.
